Who Is Watching the Moonlight Markets?

“Moonlight-market” videos show riverside towns as places where the shops never close. Who makes them, and who believes them?

Aug 5, 2024

The first time I saw a moonlight-market video, I was on the last train home. A narrator promised “the town where the shops never close,” and the camera drifted past lantern-lit stalls, fruit stacked in pyramids, and a river so calm it looked painted.

The clips run for less than a minute. A drone rises over rooftops, a vendor laughs, someone hands a stranger a paper cup of soup, and a caption promises that everything is free after midnight. None of it is quite true, and almost everyone who shares them knows it.

For months the videos followed me from one feed to another. They were reposted by travel accounts, by cooking channels, by people who had never left their own city, and each repost added a new detail: a floating bakery, a night ferry, a market that moved every full moon.

When I finally visited one of the towns in the videos, the market was real but small: eleven stalls, a generator, and a queue for dumplings. It closed at ten. The vendor who appeared in a dozen clips told me she had never been filmed with her permission.

The people making the videos are mostly not travel writers. They are editors who stitch together footage from festivals, film sets and holiday adverts, then add music and a voiceover. A single account I followed had posted the same stall under four different town names.

Viewers, it turns out, are not fooled so much as comforted. In the comments, people describe the markets they remember from childhood, argue about which soup is best, and plan trips they will probably never take. The videos work less as reporting than as a shared daydream.

That daydream has consequences. Towns named in viral clips see a rush of weekend visitors who arrive expecting lanterns and find a car park. Some councils have started running real night markets to meet the demand, which means the fiction is slowly becoming a timetable.

By the end of my trip I had stopped asking whether the moonlight markets were real. The better question was who gets to decide what a town looks like to people who have never been there, and why so many of us are happy to let a sixty-second video decide for us.
